findings.title: New abstract method order() on CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations
findings.body: The PR adds `int order();` as a new abstract method to the public `CryptoProvider` interface. keycloak-common is a published artifact and `CryptoProvider` is a ServiceLoader-loaded SPI that can be implemented outside this repository. Any existing compiled implementation used with the newer keycloak-common will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` sorts via `CryptoProvider::order`, and any source implementation stops compiling until it implements the method. Declaring it as a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would provide the new ordering capability without breaking API/binary compatibility in a shared module.

findings.title: Same-order crypto providers are now silently picked by classpath order instead of failing fast
findings.body: detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException("Multiple crypto providers loaded... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath") whenever more than one CryptoProvider was found. Now it sorts by order() and unconditionally takes the first entry. Because DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, a misconfigured classpath containing two of them — exactly the situation the old exception guarded against — no longer fails: one provider is silently chosen based on ServiceLoader/classpath ordering, which can vary between environments, and the only trace is a debug-level "Ignored crypto providers" message. In the worst case a deployment intended to run with the FIPS 140-2 provider boots with the default non-FIPS provider without anyone noticing. Consider keeping a hard failure, or at least logging a warning, when the highest order is shared by more than one provider.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore's JCA provider instead of a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the "BouncyCastle security provider" (non-FIPS or FIPS). This implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. whatever provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically SUN), which is not BouncyCastle and varies with JDK configuration. The value is exposed via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER, which other Keycloak code uses as the provider name for JCA getInstance(algorithm, provider) lookups and which CryptoIntegration.init() logs as the "java security provider", so with this provider active those lookups resolve against an arbitrary default provider rather than the documented one. Each call also instantiates a KeyStore just to obtain a Provider. If no BouncyCastle is available, returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or documenting the deviation would be more correct.

findings.title: Dead code: two discarded ASN1Encoder instances in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder objects and write rBigInteger/sBigInteger into them, but the results are never used — the returned DER sequence is built from fresh encoders in the return statement (lines 117-121). The two statements have no effect other than allocating throwaway objects and performing pointless serialization on every ES256/384/512 signature conversion, and they confuse readers about which encoders actually produce the output. They should be removed.

findings.title: New test bypasses the ServiceLoader/order mechanism that is the point of the PR
findings.body: The functional core of this PR is that AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered via META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider and is selected by CryptoIntegration only when no higher-order provider is present (DefaultCryptoProvider et al. use order 200, this one 100). The added test instantiates `new AuthzClientCryptoProvider()` directly, so a broken or missing service registration file, or an order() value that wins/loses incorrectly against DefaultCryptoProvider, would not be caught by anything. A test that loads providers through ServiceLoader/CryptoIntegration — e.g. asserting AuthzClientCryptoProvider is discoverable on its own and that DefaultCryptoProvider still wins when both are on the classpath — would cover the mechanism the PR actually introduces.
